decision: Implement multi-tenancy as owner-scoped RBAC: one framework-agnostic helper (lib/tenancy/ownership.ts, requireOwnerOrAdmin) used by HTTP routes, the WS plane and future session stores.
rationale: Owner decision on dx#119 (multi-tenant now). One helper keeps the HTTP plane, the terminal server and the substrate session store (feat/substrate-backend) on the same rule.
alternatives: Per-route ad-hoc checks (drift between planes); DB row-level security (terminal plane has no Postgres; docker/fs resources are not rows).

decision: Not-yours returns 404, never 403; resources with no owner (pre-#119) are admin-only.
rationale: Avoids disclosing other tenants' resource existence; the prototype harness already uses 404-for-not-yours; legacy resources default to the admin who ran single-tenant daax.
alternatives: 403 for not-yours (leaks existence); treating unowned as shared (exposes all legacy recordings/containers to every user).

decision: Carry RBAC and server-side settings to the terminal server as signed ticket claims (perms, admin, settings, locked); a ticketless forwarded identity is admin only via DAAX_ADMIN_USERS subjects, otherwise refused.
rationale: The terminal plane has no Postgres by design (F3 split). The ticket is already HMAC-signed, single-use and 30s TTL, so its claims are as trustworthy as its subject.
alternatives: Give the terminal server Postgres access (widens its blast radius, contradicts F3); a terminal->web internal API call per connect (new trust channel, latency).

decision: Default roles: admin = all permissions; user = terminal:exec, containers:write, recording:write, settings:write on own resources. New admin-only permission admin:settings:write for the settings policy.
rationale: Operator brief: 'admin = all; user = own resources'. settings:write now means own settings; the policy needs a separate admin permission.
alternatives: Reusing admin:users:write for the policy (conflates user management with settings).

decision: In container mode, local/shell-tmux terminals are admin-only; docker exec into a named container requires ownership of its daax.owner label.
rationale: A local shell runs inside the terminal container, which holds the docker socket and every tenant's workspace and credentials; exec into an arbitrary container named by the client bypassed tenancy.
alternatives: Keeping local shells for users (root-equivalent via docker socket).

decision: Store security settings server-side in Postgres (user_settings, settings_policy; migration 1781568000400) with admin defaults, locks and per-user overrides; keep UI preferences in localStorage; the browser keeps a localStorage cache of the security keys.
rationale: Security-relevant values must not be client-controlled. Keeping the cache means existing synchronous getSettings() callers and host-dev (no DB) are unchanged.
alternatives: Moving all settings server-side (large UI rewrite, out of scope); enforcing only in the browser (not a control).

decision: Per-user credential stores at .daax/users/<owner>/{claude,opencode}; non-destructive migration maps the existing shared store to the operator and one admin (DAAX_LEGACY_CREDENTIALS_OWNER, else first DAAX_ADMIN_USERS subject); shadow .daax with a tmpfs when a container mounts the workspace root.
rationale: Stops one shared, read-write OAuth store being mounted into every user's container. Nothing is moved or deleted, so the change is reversible and the admin keeps their login.
alternatives: Moving the legacy dir (one-way, breaks rollback); deleting it (loses the admin login); docker volume subpaths (needs Docker 26+).

decision: Record worktree ownership in git's per-worktree admin dir (.git/worktrees/<name>/daax-owner); the main worktree is shared-read, admin-only to mutate; worktree create/remove requires terminal:exec.
rationale: Invisible to git status, works without Postgres (host-dev), removed by git with the worktree.
alternatives: A Postgres table (breaks host-dev without DB, can drift from git); a file in the working tree (pollutes git status).

decision: Scope limits recorded as residual risk: shared workspace under the default mountRoot, docker socket on both planes (#501), editor/files/code-server share the workspace, skip-permissions lock only strips the launch flag.
rationale: Each needs its own design (per-tenant workspaces, docker-socket proxy) beyond dx#119's direction; stated in docs/multi-tenancy.md and the PR.

decision: Make transcripts (/api/transcripts*), the Watchtower attention board (/api/watchtower/*) and its WS stream (?stream=attention), and the Agent View proxy (/api/agentview/*) admin-only.
rationale: They expose the operator's transcripts and every agent's live prompts/tool output, and their sessions carry no daax owner, so they cannot be owner-filtered; the unowned-is-admin-only rule fails closed.
alternatives: Leaving them open to all authenticated users (cross-tenant leak of prompts and file contents); owner-filtering via Watchtower (needs an owner on Watchtower sessions — follow-up).

decision: Supersedes gh-119-multi-tenant-008: record worktree owners in daax's own state dir (~/.daax/worktree-owners.json, the daax-recordings volume in container mode) keyed by canonical path, not in .git/worktrees/<name>/.
rationale: Cross-provider review (Codex) showed git metadata is writable by every tenant's agent container under the shared workspace, so an owner stored there can be rewritten to claim another tenant's worktree. The state dir is never mounted into agent containers and still needs no Postgres.
alternatives: Postgres table (breaks host-dev without DB); git metadata (tenant-writable — rejected).

decision: Refuse non-admin terminal mounts that canonically resolve inside <workspace>/.daax, in addition to the tmpfs shadow on whole-workspace mounts.
rationale: Cross-provider review showed a direct mount of .daax/users/<other>/claude passed workspace confinement. The check uses the existing realpath-based isValidPath so planted symlinks cannot bypass it.
alternatives: Moving credential stores out of the workspace (needs a host path the terminal plane does not have, or Docker volume subpaths).

decision: When DAAX_WS_TOKEN_SECRET is configured, a WS upgrade with only a forwarded identity (no ticket) gets no permissions, admins included; the DAAX_ADMIN_USERS fallback applies only when ticketing is off (host-dev behind Traefik).
rationale: Cross-provider review showed a bare forwarded admin skipped the signed perms and settings locks. With ticketing on the client always mints a ticket, so the signed claims can be the only authority.
alternatives: Keeping the allowlist fallback with ticketing on (lets a DB-revoked admin or a locked subject bypass by omitting the ticket).

decision: Make POST /api/code-server (launch) admin-only and record the deploy-topology code-server route as a blocking follow-up.
rationale: code-server is an --auth none IDE over the whole workspace including .daax credential stores; it cannot be owner-scoped. In the deploy compose Traefik routes to it directly, outside the app's control.
alternatives: Leaving launch open (shared IDE over every tenant's files).

decision: Decide the .daax tmpfs shadow on canonical paths (shadow whenever .daax canonically lies inside the mount, and only when it exists) instead of lexical equality with HOST_WORKSPACE_PATH.
rationale: Second cross-provider review: a symlink aliasing the workspace root passed confinement but skipped the lexical shadow, exposing every credential store. Requiring existence avoids Docker creating an empty .daax mountpoint in the host workspace.
alternatives: Rejecting any alias of the root (also sound, but the canonical shadow covers it without refusing legitimate root mounts).

decision: Apply the tenant mount boundary (admin-set mountRoot, no source inside or containing .daax, canonical checks) to testcontainers and compose bind mounts for non-admins, before anything is created or stored.
rationale: Second cross-provider review: these APIs confined binds only to the shared workspace, so a mountRoot-confined user could bind another tenant's directory, and testcontainers get no tmpfs shadow.
alternatives: Enforcing inside the plugin's docker-client (it has no principal); leaving it to the shared-workspace validator (bypass).
